video_title: Mark Skousen: Why He's Still 100% Invested at All-Time Highs
gist: Economist and newsletter writer Mark Skousen tells Wealthion's Maggie Lake he is 100% invested at all-time highs because his gross output measure shows business-to-business spending growing faster than GDP, corporate profits are at records, and AI is driving a technology-led 'golden era.' He simultaneously treats inflation as a permanent policy regime that forces investors to compound 8-10% a year just to stand still, and warns the $40 trillion debt, $2 trillion deficit and $7 trillion of Treasury refinancing mean the US will eventually hit a wall. His portfolio answer is zero bonds, dividend-growing financials and energy, miners and royalty companies rather than physical metal, copper/uranium/blockchain equities, and a pre-defined exit trigger: levered hedge funds or private equity firms going bankrupt in a way that spreads.

themes.theme: Gross output and the technology-led bull case

insights.claim: Mark Skousen argues GDP understates the economy because it omits the business-to-business supply chain, which by his gross output measure is larger than GDP itself.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Investors tracking only GDP miss the B2B capex cycle; gross output can flag supplier and industrial earnings turns before consumer data does.
insights.quote: GDP leaves out the supply chain, which is bigger than GDP itself

insights.claim: Business-to-business spending is now growing faster than GDP after two years of tariff- and pandemic-driven supply chain strain, and corporate profits are at record highs, which Skousen says the bears are ignoring.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A B2B-led acceleration with record profits means the all-time-high market has an earnings foundation, weakening the pure multiple-expansion bubble case.

insights.claim: AI-driven technology is producing new productivity and record stock prices but has not helped the labor market, leaving employment and overall economic growth sluggish.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A market rising on productivity while jobs stay weak keeps political pressure on the Fed to cut even as market rates rise, a persistent policy tension to trade around.

themes.theme: Permanent inflation as policy, not cycle

insights.claim: Skousen frames US inflation as a permanent policy regime rather than a cyclical event, because the Federal Reserve replaced price stability with Bernanke's 2% target while the country runs fiat money and chronic deficits, producing a post-World War II price level that looks like a hockey stick and has never come back down.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: If inflation is structural policy rather than a cycle, cash and fixed-rate bonds are a permanent tax and real-asset exposure becomes a baseline allocation, not a hedge.
insights.quote: We have a permanent inflation policy. That is our policy.

insights.claim: Skousen sets an explicit investor hurdle rate of roughly 8 to 10 percent net worth growth per year simply to stay ahead of structural inflation.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: That hurdle mathematically rules out most cash and investment-grade bond allocations for anyone trying to preserve purchasing power.
insights.quote: you need to see an increase in your net worth by I think 8 to 10% a year just to stay ahead of this whole inflation problem

insights.claim: Skousen points to gold and Bitcoin elevated, copper at an all-time high and uranium prices rising as evidence that inflation is showing up broadly across commodities, not just in groceries, gasoline and housing.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Breadth across unrelated commodities argues the move is monetary rather than a single-commodity squeeze, supporting a basket approach over single-name bets.

themes.theme: Warsh's Fed and the fiscal wall

insights.claim: Skousen expects Kevin Warsh to postpone rate hikes as long as possible ahead of the midterm elections, with all bets off afterward, and argues Trump cannot get lower rates because market rates are rising and may even force the Fed to hike.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Trades that depend on easy policy have a defined shelf life: the window closes after November, making post-midterm rate risk the key calendar event.
insights.quote: I think he's going to postpone as long as possible the raising of rates, but all bets are off after the midterms.

insights.claim: Skousen is optimistic on Kevin Warsh because Warsh sees himself as a Paul Volcker and has returned to watching the money supply, which Jerome Powell explicitly abandoned while allowing money supply to grow 40% in a couple of years after the pandemic.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A money-supply-watching Fed chair raises the odds of tighter-than-expected policy after the midterms and makes M2 the leading indicator to track, not labor prints.

insights.claim: The US Treasury has to refinance $7 trillion this year, and Skousen warns foreign governments could shift at the margin into gold, Bitcoin or Swiss francs instead of Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Refinancing scale plus reserve-asset substitution is the mechanism for a rate spike; watch auction tails and official-sector gold buying as the tell.
insights.quote: the Treasury has to refinance $7 trillion this year

insights.claim: Skousen calls Scott Bessent's Treasury buyback program a short-term fool's errand designed to hold rates artificially low through the midterms, and says it is already failing because interest rates keep moving higher.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: If buybacks are not working, the rate-suppression support many equity bulls are counting on disappears and long-end yields drift higher.

insights.claim: Skousen says a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion deficit at full employment violates even Keynesian doctrine, and invokes Buchanan and Tullock's public choice theory to argue deficits are structurally inevitable because spending is popular with individual congressmen while taxes are not.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Treat fiscal consolidation as a low-probability scenario when pricing long bonds; the incentive structure, not the personnel, drives the deficits.
insights.quote: when you're at full employment you should be running a surplus not a $2 trillion deficit

themes.theme: Yen carry trade and pre-defined crisis triggers

insights.claim: Skousen identifies the yen-dollar carry trade as the leading black swan candidate: institutions borrowed yen at about 1 percent to buy US Treasuries yielding 4 to 5 percent, must repay in a sharply weaker yen, and Scott Bessent intervened by buying yen to stop private equity firms from going under in a repeat of Long-Term Capital Management in 1998.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Yen strength is the trigger to watch, and the scale of official intervention is a proxy for how stressed the levered Treasury carry position actually is.

insights.claim: Skousen argues inflation cannot be brought down without bursting bubbles such as the carry trade, making successful disinflation itself the risk event.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Positioning for disinflation should include tail hedges on levered credit rather than assuming a benign soft landing for risk assets.

insights.claim: Skousen's stated trigger for cutting equity exposure is hedge funds and private equity firms declaring bankruptcy in a way that starts spreading quickly, the Lehman Brothers pattern of 2008 rather than a simple index drawdown.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A concrete, observable de-risking signal: monitor credit events at levered financial intermediaries, not price action alone.

insights.claim: Even in a crisis Skousen would not exit the market entirely but would build a larger cash position while holding income-producing stocks, citing Richard Russell's rule that the bear-market winner is whoever loses the least.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic bear-market objective of relative loss minimization via dividend cushion plus partial cash, instead of attempting to time an exit.
insights.quote: in a bare market the winner is he who loses the least

themes.theme: Staying fully invested and detecting the turn

insights.claim: Skousen is 100 percent invested apart from cash for special situations, and justifies holding through known risks by arguing modern liquidity lets him exit equities instantly.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: The entire position rests on liquidity being available at the moment of stress, historically the first assumption to break in a crisis.
insights.quote: because we can get out of equities at any time with the click of a button, my dear

insights.claim: Skousen refuses to act on calendar-dated crash calls such as a predicted 2027 market massacre, saying he will stay fully invested until the market is actually and materially falling.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A trend-following discipline that accepts being late in exchange for never being early, and that only breaks on confirmed price damage.

insights.claim: Skousen applies Humphrey Neill's contrary-opinion rule that the public is right during trends but wrong at both ends, noting those reversals occur only about once every ten years, as in 1999 and March 2009.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Because reversals are rare, fading the crowd mid-trend is a losing strategy; contrarianism only pays at genuine extremes.
insights.quote: the public is right during the trends but wrong at both ends

insights.claim: Skousen holds no bond positions at all because rising rates mean falling bond prices, substituting dividend-paying stocks with rising dividend policies that out-yield Treasuries and bank CDs.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: An explicit rejection of the 60/40 model: the income sleeve moves from duration risk to equity dividend growth, accepting equity beta as the trade-off.

insights.claim: Skousen's income holdings span financials and energy, including Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Main Street Capital and Enterprise Products around 6 to 7 percent and Williams at 3 percent, all above the S&P 500 dividend yield, with Main Street Capital singled out as the only stock paying both a monthly and a quarterly dividend, roughly 1 percent of its private-company portfolio in default and expected returns of 10 to 20 percent a year including dividends.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable high-yield basket concentrated in midstream energy and financials, with a BDC offering indirect pre-IPO private-company exposure.
insights.quote: It's the only stock that pays a monthly and quarterly dividend.

insights.claim: Skousen avoids double-digit dividend yields because those payouts are likely to be cut in a crisis, but says a stock that raises its dividend during a correction should be held because it signals recovery.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Two operational rules for an income screen: treat double-digit yields as distress, and use dividend declarations during drawdowns as the hold-versus-sell test.

insights.claim: Skousen expresses commodity views through equities rather than the commodity itself, preferring miners and royalty companies such as Franco Nevada because miners sit at the earliest, highest-beta stage of production, while still recommending physical gold and silver coins despite theft and storage risk; he targets an overall portfolio beta only slightly above 1.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Royalty companies deliver commodity upside with lower operational beta than miners, and the dividend sleeve is sized to offset the speculative sleeve.

insights.claim: Skousen ties his commodity and energy positioning directly to data centers: Southern Copper with copper at an all-time high, uranium and small modular nuclear plants over expensive wind and solar, and elevated oil and gas prices persisting because data centers need them until nuclear can take over years from now.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Copper, uranium and energy equities are second-derivative AI trades with commodity floors and less model-obsolescence risk than semiconductor names.
insights.quote: you need oil and gas to fund the energy needs of the data centers

insights.claim: Skousen gets Bitcoin exposure through BLOK, an ETF holding blockchain and crypto companies, rather than owning Bitcoin directly, arguing the operating companies are a leveraged way to profit and have outperformed Bitcoin itself.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: An operating-leverage route to crypto beta worth benchmarking against spot before choosing how to express a crypto view.

themes.theme: AI capex risk, IPO mechanics and speculation sizing

insights.claim: Skousen says tech stocks could fall in half and still be overvalued, yet he continues to hold positions in them because the trend is intact.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: A trend-follower knowingly holding assets he believes are fundamentally overpriced, which makes his exit trigger, not the valuation, the thing to monitor.
insights.quote: tech stocks could fall in half and still be overvalued

insights.claim: Skousen warns a significant correction could hit before the billions Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and other tech companies are pouring into AI data centers pay off, noting that capex is consuming huge amounts of their cash flow and that SpaceX is currently losing money because of xAI.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Frames AI spending as a short-term cash flow loss for a long-term gain, so free cash flow compression is the metric that would break the rally.

insights.claim: Skousen would buy Anthropic or OpenAI only through pre-IPO private placements the way Ron Baron got into Tesla and SpaceX early, because once the IPO arrives insiders are selling and the retail buyer is the one holding what he calls the burning match.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Sets the rule for the coming AI IPO wave: pre-listing access matters more than the name, and post-IPO buyers are structurally disadvantaged.
insights.quote: Once the IPO comes out, I mean, that's when the insiders are starting to sell, and it's really hard to make money.

insights.claim: Skousen's speculation rule is strict position sizing rather than avoidance: never back up the truck on a story stock, because a small position can still make a lot of money and you will be glad it was small if the thesis fails, which is how he plays loss-making AI names like CoreWeave, a nickel exploration play and small-cap drone makers benefiting from defense spending instead of Lockheed Martin.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Gives a repeatable way to hold convex exposure to speculative AI and defense themes without the concentration that ruins a portfolio when one fails.

insights.claim: Skousen names Trump's tariff trade war and the ongoing Middle East war as the two policies actively working against the market, saying tariffs unambiguously raise costs and that Trump may have bitten off more than he can chew, with the midterms as the verdict.
insights.speaker: Mark Skousen
insights.so_what: Two identifiable political risk vectors whose escalation or resolution would move corporate margins and energy prices in opposite directions.
